---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide.md
description: What Frensense is, what it scans, and where to go next.
---

# Frensense overview

Frensense is a static application security testing (SAST) scanner. It reads
your source code, follows untrusted input through the program, and reports a
finding only when that input can reach a dangerous call. Every finding shows
the path it took, with file and line positions, so you can check it yourself.

It is one binary. Scanning, watch mode, the AI-agent server (`frensense mcp`)
and the editor server (`frensense lsp`) are all subcommands of `frensense`.

::: warning What to expect
Frensense is young and deliberately conservative about what it reports, which
means it **misses real vulnerabilities**. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python it
currently finds 38% of the vulnerable cases, and it finds none of the cases
for cross-site scripting, weak randomness, XML external entities, LDAP
injection or trust-boundary violations. See
the [benchmark record](/architecture/benchmarks) for the numbers, and treat a
clean scan as "nothing found", not "nothing there".
:::

## Choose your path

| I want to... | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| Scan a project once | [Install](/guide/installation), then [Your first scan](/guide/first-scan) |
| Fail a pull request on new findings | [CI and agent gating](/guide/github-actions) |
| Let an AI coding agent check its own changes | [AI agents (MCP)](/guide/mcp) |
| See findings in my editor | [Editors (LSP)](/guide/lsp) |
| Look up a flag or an exit code | [CLI reference](/guide/cli) |
| Add knowledge about my framework | [Bundles](/bundles), then [How teaching works](/guide/teachability) |
| Help improve the engine | [Engine Blindness Challenges](/challenges) |

## What it scans

| Language | File extensions |
| --- | --- |
| TypeScript | `.ts` `.tsx` `.mts` `.cts` |
| JavaScript | `.js` `.jsx` `.mjs` `.cjs` |
| Python | `.py` `.pyi` `.pyw` |
| Go | `.go` |
| Rust | `.rs` |
| C | `.c` `.h` |
| Vue | `.vue` single-file components (early support) |

C++ is not supported. Files in other languages are skipped.

## What it reports

57 built-in rules, each with a stable id and a CWE number. Run
`frensense explain` to list them, or `frensense explain <rule-id>` for the
explanation and fix advice of one.

* **Taint flows (`taint.*`, 30 rules):** untrusted input reaching a dangerous
  call. These include SQL, NoSQL, command, code, template, LDAP and XPath
  injection, path traversal, SSRF, open redirect, XSS, unsafe deserialization,
  XXE, prototype pollution and regular-expression denial of service.
* **Checks (`check.*`, 27 rules):** problems that do not need a source, such as
  weak hashes and ciphers, missing cookie flags, insecure transport, and the
  memory-safety checks (use after free, double free, out-of-bounds access,
  integer overflow in an allocation size, memory leaks).

A rule existing does not mean it works on every framework. Detection depends
on the engine knowing the framework's sources and sinks, which is what
[bundles](/bundles) add.

## How a finding is produced

1. Each file is parsed and converted to a small intermediate form.
2. The engine builds a graph of how values move between variables, functions
   and objects across the whole project.
3. It asks one question per dangerous call: can a value from an untrusted
   source reach this argument without passing through a sanitizer or a guard?
4. If yes, you get a finding with the path. If the engine cannot tell (for
   example, a value comes from code it cannot see), it stays quiet rather than
   guessing. `frensense --explain` lists those silent spots.

The same input always gives the same output. There is no model, no network
call and no sampling in the scan. See [Architecture](/architecture/) for the
details.

## Status

Frensense is at version v0.8.0. The
documentation for the earlier 1.x line is kept at [/v1/](/v1/). Version 2
is a rebuild of the engine.

## Summary for assistants

Frensense (`frensense` on crates.io, `@friehub/frensense` on npm) is a
GPL-3.0 deterministic dataflow scanner for TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go,
Rust, C and Vue files. It reports taint paths from untrusted sources to
dangerous calls. It is not a replacement for a full SAST suite: detection
coverage is limited (see /architecture/benchmarks), so describe results as
"findings" and a clean scan as "nothing found".

Useful for: CI gates (`frensense . --compare-baseline baseline.json`), scanning
an unfamiliar repository, checking an AI agent's own edits through MCP
(`frensense mcp`; tools `frensense_audit`, `frensense_scan_file`,
`frensense_diff`), and editor diagnostics (`frensense lsp`).

Install: `cargo install frensense` or `npm install -g @friehub/frensense`.
One binary, three surfaces; there is no separate MCP or LSP package.

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/installation.md

# Install

Frensense is one binary named `frensense`. Pick the route that fits your
machine, then run `frensense --version` to check it worked.

| Route | Needs | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm | Node.js 18 or newer | `npm install -g @friehub/frensense` |
| No install | Node.js 18 or newer | `npx @friehub/frensense .` |
| Cargo | Rust 1.95 or newer | `cargo install frensense` |
| Release download | nothing | see below |

## npm

The npm package carries prebuilt binaries, so you do not need a Rust
compiler. It supports Linux x64, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon) and Windows
x64.

```bash
npm install -g @friehub/frensense
frensense --version
```

The `frensense` command from npm is a small launcher around the native
binary. Every subcommand (`watch`, `mcp`, `lsp`, ...) works the same way.

## Cargo

```bash
cargo install frensense
```

This compiles the binary and puts it in `~/.cargo/bin`. It needs Rust 1.95 or
newer, and takes a few minutes.

## Release download

Each [GitHub release](https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2/releases)
attaches one binary per platform, named after its Rust target:

| Platform | File |
| --- | --- |
| Linux x64 | `frensense-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` |
| macOS Intel | `frensense-x86_64-apple-darwin` |
| macOS Apple Silicon | `frensense-aarch64-apple-darwin` |
| Windows x64 | `frensense-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.exe` |

There is no Linux arm64 build yet. On Linux x64:

```bash
curl -L -o frensense \
  https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2/releases/latest/download/frensense-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
chmod +x frensense
sudo mv frensense /usr/local/bin/
```

Releases are built by a GitHub Actions workflow that also produces a SLSA
provenance file (`*.intoto.jsonl`) for the binaries. You can check a download
against it with [slsa-verifier](https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-verifier).

## Check the install

```bash
frensense --version     # prints: frensense 0.8.0
frensense --help        # lists every flag and subcommand
```

If a scan ends with `Status: Failed analysis` and a warning about
"unsupported or absent source input", the folder holds no
[supported files](/guide/#what-it-scans). Try it inside a project that has a
`.py`, `.ts`, `.js`, `.go`, `.rs` or `.c` file.

## Build from source

Only needed if you want to change the engine:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2.git
cd frensense-v2
cargo build --release
```

The binary is `target/release/frensense`. See
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
before opening a pull request.

## Next

[Run your first scan](/guide/first-scan).

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/first-scan.md
description: >-
  Scan a small vulnerable app, read the finding, and learn what the exit code
  means.
---

# Your first scan

This takes about two minutes. You need [Frensense installed](/guide/installation).

## 1. Make something to scan

Save this as `app.py` in an empty folder. It is a Flask app with two
vulnerabilities: user input goes straight into a shell command and into an SQL
query.

```python
import os
import sqlite3
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/ping")
def ping():
    host = request.args.get("host")
    return os.popen("ping -c 1 " + host).read()

@app.route("/user")
def user():
    uid = request.args.get("id")
    db = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    return str(db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + uid).fetchall())
```

## 2. Scan it

```bash
frensense .
```

You get one block per finding, then a summary:

```text
[CRITICAL] OS command injection: `request.get` reaches `popen`
  --> app.py:10:12 (in `ping`)

     |
   9 |     host = request.args.get("host")
  10 |     return os.popen("ping -c 1 " + host).read()
     |            ^^^^^^^^
     |
  = rule: taint.command-injection  (CWE-78)
  = why:  Attacker-supplied text reaches a shell or process launcher and can run other commands.
  = fix:  Pass arguments as a list without a shell, and validate the value against an allowlist.

[CRITICAL] SQL injection: `request.get` reaches `execute`
  --> app.py:16:16 (in `user`)
  ...
Total Findings: 2
```

## 3. Read a finding

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `[CRITICAL]` | Severity: `critical`, `warning` or `info`. |
| `` `request.get` reaches `popen` `` | The **source** (where untrusted data enters) and the **sink** (the dangerous call it reaches). |
| `--> app.py:10:12 (in `ping`)` | File, line and column of the sink, and the function it is in. |
| `rule: taint.command-injection (CWE-78)` | The stable rule id and its CWE number. |
| `why` and `fix` | A one-line explanation and the usual remedy. |

To see every step between source and sink, add `--show-flows`. To read about a
rule without scanning anything, run `frensense explain taint.command-injection`.

## 4. Fix them and scan again

For the command, accept only known hosts before the value reaches the shell.
For the query, pass the value as a bound parameter:

```python
@app.route("/ping")
def ping():
    host = request.args.get("host")
    if host not in ("example.com", "example.org"):
        return "unknown host", 400
    return os.popen("ping -c 1 " + host).read()

@app.route("/user")
def user():
    uid = request.args.get("id")
    db = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    return str(db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (uid,)).fetchall())
```

Run `frensense .` again and the scan reports nothing.

::: tip The scanner learns what counts as safe
Frensense clears a finding when the value passes through something it knows is
a sanitizer or a guard. Today that includes a literal allow-list check like the
one above, `shlex.quote`, and bound query parameters. It does not recognise
every validation: a `re.fullmatch` check, for example, still leaves the
finding. If a fix you believe in does not clear a finding, that is an engine
gap worth reporting, and a good [challenge](/challenges) to take on.
:::

## What the exit code means

Frensense exits with `0` after a normal scan **even when it found something**.
That keeps a first run from breaking your shell or a script. To make findings
fail a command, ask for it:

```bash
frensense . --strict    # exit 1 if there is any finding
```

For CI you usually want the gentler rule "fail only on findings that are new",
which is [baseline gating](/guide/github-actions).

## Other output formats

```bash
frensense . --json                    # one JSON object, for scripts
frensense . --sarif -o results.sarif  # SARIF 2.1.0, for code-scanning tools
frensense . --github                  # GitHub Actions annotations
```

## Where to go next

* Findings in pull requests: [CI and agent gating](/guide/github-actions)
* Every flag: [CLI reference](/guide/cli)
* Missing a finding you expected? The engine may not know your framework yet.
  See [Bundles](/bundles).

# CLI reference

This page matches `frensense --help` for version 0.8.0. If your installed
version is older or newer, `frensense --help` is the final word.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `frensense <path>` | Scan a file or folder and print findings. Use `.` for the current folder. With no arguments it prints the help text. |
| `frensense watch [path]` | Re-scan when files change and print only new findings. |
| `frensense explain [rule-id]` | Explain one rule (CWE, why, fix). With no id, list all rules. |
| `frensense mcp` | Run the MCP server for AI agents. See [AI agents](/guide/mcp). |
| `frensense lsp` | Run the editor server. See [Editors](/guide/lsp). |
| `frensense bundle <corpus> [out.frc]` | Compile labelled examples into a `.frc` bundle. |
| `frensense bundle info <file.frc>` | Show what a bundle contains (`--json` for machine output). |
| `frensense lint <corpus>` | Check corpus examples before they are bundled. |

Everything is in the one binary. There is no separate MCP or LSP package.

### When a folder has the same name as a command

A path that exists wins over a subcommand name, so a repository containing a
`mcp/` or `watch/` folder can still be scanned with the bare word. Each mode has
a spelling that cannot be confused:

| To do this | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Start the MCP server | `frensense --mcp` |
| Watch a path | `frensense watch <path>` (the path makes it unambiguous) |
| Compile a bundle | `frensense bundle <corpus> [out.frc]` |
| Lint a corpus | `frensense lint <corpus>` |
| List all rules | `frensense --list-rules` |
| Explain one rule | `frensense --explain-rule <rule-id>` |

`frensense lsp` is always the server, because editors start it without a
terminal and a silent scan there would be a bug, not an ambiguity.

## Scan options

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-b`, `--bundle <file>` | Load a `.frc` [bundle](/bundles) for this scan. `--corpus-bundle` is an older spelling of the same flag. |
| `-l`, `--language <lang>` | Scan one language only: `c`, `go`, `javascript`, `python`, `rust`, `typescript`, `vue`. |
| `-s`, `--severity <level>` | Lowest severity to report: `critical`, `warning` or `info`. Default `warning`, so `info` findings are hidden unless you ask. |
| `-p`, `--profile <name>` | `default`, `recommended` or `strict`. `strict` also reports hygiene rules such as function complexity. |
| `--hygiene` | Report hygiene rules (for example, function complexity) under any profile. |
| `--max-complexity <n>` | Complexity ceiling before a function is reported (default 25). |
| `--diff-only` | Report only findings on lines changed since the last git commit. Changed files are still analysed whole, because a change can make an old line reachable. |

## Output options

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-o`, `--output <file>` | Write the report to a file instead of printing it. |
| `-f`, `--format <fmt>` | `text`, `json`, `sarif` or `github`. |
| `--json` | One JSON object with an `advisories` list. Same as `--format json`. |
| `--sarif` | SARIF 2.1.0. Same as `--format sarif`. |
| `--github` | GitHub Actions annotation commands. Same as `--format github`. |
| `--show-flows` | In text output, list each step from source to sink. (JSON and SARIF always include the path.) |
| `--explain` | Also list sink arguments that produced no finding and why (printed to stderr). |
| `--explain-json <file>` | Write those silent sink arguments to a file as JSON. Implies `--explain`. |

### The JSON report

`--json` prints a single JSON object, not one object per line. The fields you
will most often use:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `advisory_count` | Number of findings. |
| `advisories` | The findings. Each has `rule_id`, `severity`, `title`, `file_path`, `line`, `column`, `fingerprint` and `taint_steps`. |
| `clean` | `true` when there are no findings. |
| `analysis_incomplete` | Reasons the scan may have missed things (unsupported or partly parsed files, safety limits). Check this before you trust a clean result. |
| `schema_version` | Version of this report format. |

## Gating options

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--strict` | Exit 1 if there is **any** finding. |
| `--emit-baseline <file>` | Save the current findings as a baseline. |
| `--compare-baseline <file>` | Exit 1 only if there are findings that are not in the baseline. |

::: warning Do not combine `--strict` with `--compare-baseline`
`--strict` fails on any finding, including ones already in the baseline, so the
pair fails every run. Use `--compare-baseline` on its own for a regression gate.
See [CI and agent gating](/guide/github-actions).
:::

## Exit codes

| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The scan finished. Findings do not change this unless you ask for it. |
| `1` | `--strict` and at least one finding; or `--compare-baseline` found a new finding; or an error such as an unreadable bundle file. |
| `2` | The command line was wrong (unknown flag, invalid severity, and so on). |

## Environment

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` | Default `.frc` bundle for the MCP and LSP servers. The CLI scan uses `-b` instead. |

A file named `frensense-corpus.frc` in the folder being scanned is loaded
automatically when no `-b` is given.

## Explaining a rule

Every finding carries a stable rule id (`taint.sql-injection`,
`check.weak-hash`, ...). `frensense explain <rule-id>` prints what it means:

```console
$ frensense explain taint.path-traversal
taint.path-traversal  Path traversal
  CWE:  CWE-22  https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html
  why:  Attacker-supplied path segments can reach files outside the intended directory.
  fix:  Resolve the path, then check it stays inside the allowed base directory; prefer fixed names.
```

Rules that came from a bundle describe themselves from the bundle's data. Pass
`-b` to explain or list them:

```console
$ frensense explain policy.redirect-challenge -b learned.frc
```

## Version and identity

`frensense --version` prints the version. `frensense --version --json` also
prints the bundle format the binary reads and the size of the built-in
knowledge pack.

## Corpus commands

`frensense lint <corpus>` takes `--strict`, `--json`, `--coverage`,
`--no-gate`, `--classes <file>`, `--advisories <file>`, `--require-heldout`
and `--dup-threshold <0..1>`. It exits 1 when it finds an error. The
[authoring guide](/corpus/authoring) explains what each check means.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/github-actions.md
description: Fail pull requests on new findings, annotate them, and gate AI agents.
---

# CI and agent gating

Frensense is designed for a split workflow: **AI agents fix code, CI judges
it.** This guide wires the two halves together with the CLI surface
(`--github` for CI annotations, baselines for regression gating) and shows
where the MCP and LSP surfaces plug in. Every mechanism here shares one
finding-identity scheme, so "the same bug" means the same thing on both
sides.

## The model

```
┌──────────┐  frensense mcp        ┌──────────────┐
│ AI agent │──────────────────────▶│ per-change   │
│          │   frensense_diff      │ gate (fast)  │
└────┬─────┘                       └──────────────┘
     │ edit/commit                          │
     ▼                                      ▼
┌──────────┐  pull request          ┌──────────────┐
│   CI     │───────────────────────▶│ baseline +   │
│          │   frensense --github   │ annotations  │
└──────────┘                        └──────────────┘
```

* **The agent gates its own change** before committing with
  `frensense_diff`: only findings on the change's added lines are
  reported, so pre-existing debt never blocks it.
* **CI enforces the invariant** with a baseline (`--compare-baseline`): a merged
  change can never *increase* the number of findings, even as the
  codebase churns.
* Both sides speak the same finding identity (stable fingerprints), so
  an agent fix and a CI pass are provably about the same finding.

## 1. CI workflow: annotations + baseline gate

### One-time: capture the baseline

Baselines record the findings that exist *today*; from then on, CI only
fails on findings that are **new**. Findings whose lines shift after
unrelated edits are recognized as the same finding (stable fingerprints
exclude line/column), so the baseline does not rot as the codebase moves.

```bash
cargo install frensense   # or download the release binary

frensense . --emit-baseline .frensense/baseline.json
git add .frensense/baseline.json && git commit -m "chore: frensense baseline"
```

Commit the baseline file: it is the shared contract between the agent
and CI about what debt is accepted.

### The workflow

`.github/workflows/frensense.yml`:

```yaml
name: Frensense

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      # Required for actions/checkout on pull_request to read the merge commit
      checks: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@fbc6f3992d24b796d5a048ff273f7fcc4a7b6c09 # v4.3.0

      - name: Install frensense
        run: |
          curl -L https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2/releases/latest/download/frensense-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu \
            -o /usr/local/bin/frensense && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/frensense

      - name: Baseline gate (fail on new findings)
        run: |
          frensense . \
            --compare-baseline .frensense/baseline.json \
            --github

      - name: Strict full scan (optional hard gate)
        run: frensense . --github --strict
        continue-on-error: true   # flip to false once TPR debt is burned down
```

### What each flag does

| flag | behavior | exit code |
|---|---|---|
| `--compare-baseline <file>` | fails only on findings whose fingerprint is not in the baseline | `1` on new findings, `0` otherwise |
| `--github` / `--github-annotations` | prints one `::error\|warning\|notice file=…,line=…,col=…,title=…::message` command per finding; GitHub renders these inline on the PR's Files Changed tab | unchanged |
| `--strict` | fails on *any* finding (ignores the baseline) | `1` if any finding exists |

Combine them: `--compare-baseline --github` fails the job on regressions
*and* annotates every finding in the diff view. The baseline gate and the
annotation rendering are independent: annotations appear for all current
findings so reviewers see the accepted debt in context, while the exit
code reflects only the regression verdict.

Recommended policy: **baseline gate as the failing step; strict scan with
`continue-on-error: true` as a visibility step** until the accepted debt
is burned down, then flip it to a hard gate. This gives agents a green
path for fixing existing findings without ever letting the total increase.

### Updating the baseline

When an agent (or human) fixes findings, shrink the baseline in the same
PR:

```bash
frensense . --emit-baseline .frensense/baseline.json
git add .frensense/baseline.json
```

Reviewers should treat a baseline-shrinking diff the same way they treat
a test-count-increasing diff: as a positive. If a PR *grows* the
baseline, that is the agent asking to accept new debt; reject or inspect.

**Migration note:** baselines captured before stable IDs landed
(pre-`FRN-` fingerprints, which hashed the line number) must be
regenerated once, as above. After that one regeneration, comparisons are
shift-stable.

## 2. Agent-side gating (pre-commit)

The MCP server is the agent's primary surface (see
[docs/MCP_USAGE.md](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/mcp) for the full walkthrough). The pattern
that keeps PRs green:

1. **Edit.**
2. **Gate the change**: call `frensense_diff` with `repo` set to the
   workspace. It runs `git diff HEAD` (plus untracked files), scans every
   touched file, and reports only findings on added lines.
3. **Fix until `clean: true`.** The result's `stable_ids` name exactly
   which findings the change introduces; after a fix, the ID disappearing
   is proof that specific finding is resolved, regardless of how lines
   moved in between.
4. **Commit.** CI re-runs the same engine over the whole tree; because
   the agent's change introduced nothing new, the baseline gate passes.

For agents working through an editor instead of the MCP, the LSP surface
([docs/LSP_USAGE.md](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/lsp)) shows the same findings with the same
IDs as diagnostics on save.

### Without MCP: plain shell

An agent that only has shell access gets identical semantics from the
CLI. New findings relative to the baseline, with GitHub annotation
formatting on stdout:

```bash
frensense . --compare-baseline .frensense/baseline.json --github
echo "exit=$?"   # 0 = no regressions, 1 = new findings
```

Or gate just the changed files (works without a committed baseline):

```bash
frensense . --diff-only --github
```

## 3. Watch mode: local inner loop

While developing with an agent running in a terminal, a second terminal
running the watcher turns it into a live gate:

```bash
frensense watch .
```

* Re-scans changed files every 500 ms and prints **only new findings**
  (fingerprint-set diff between rounds), so the stream goes quiet when a
  fix lands.
* Accepts the same flags as a one-shot scan, e.g.
  `frensense watch . --corpus-bundle frensense-corpus.frc`.
* Ctrl-C to stop; exit code follows the usual convention.

## 4. Finding identity across surfaces

A finding has one fingerprint everywhere. Concretely:

| surface | where the identity appears |
|---|---|
| CLI text | stable ID printed in regression output (`FRN-…`) |
| CLI JSON / MCP advisories | `fingerprint` field on every advisory |
| MCP diff/scan_file results | top-level `stable_ids` array |
| LSP diagnostics | `code` field of each diagnostic |
| baseline file | the `fingerprint` field of each stored advisory |

The fingerprint hashes semantic coordinates only (file, rule/sink,
enclosing function, source), never line numbers. Consequences:

* Inserting/deleting unrelated code **moves** the finding but keeps its
  identity: baselines don't churn, issue links stay valid.
* Renaming the enclosing function, changing the sink, or fixing the call
  **changes** the identity: it is a genuinely different code state.
* `frensense_diff` gates on added *lines*; the baseline gate gates on
  added *fingerprints*. Together they bound both directions: the agent
  can't add new findings (diff gate) and can't quietly break existing
  fixes (baseline gate).

## 5. Reference CI recipes

### Minimal (annotations only, never fails)

```yaml
- run: frensense . --github
```

### Agent-friendly (default)

```yaml
- run: frensense . --compare-baseline .frensense/baseline.json --github
```

Fails on regressions, annotates everything, tolerates line churn.

### Hard gate (debt burned down)

```yaml
- run: frensense . --github --strict
```

Fails on any finding. Use after the accepted debt reaches zero.

### Bundle-aware

```yaml
- run: >
    frensense . --corpus-bundle frensense-corpus.frc
    --compare-baseline .frensense/baseline.json --github
```

Use the same bundle in CI as the agent's MCP server does; learned facts
change what the engine can see, and both sides must agree on reality.

## See also

* [AI agents (MCP)](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/mcp): agent tool surface and an end-to-end session
* [Editors (LSP)](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/lsp): editor surface
* [CLI reference](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/cli): every flag and exit code

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/mcp.md
description: >-
  Run Frensense as an MCP server so AI coding agents can check their own
  changes.
---

# AI agents (MCP)

`frensense mcp` exposes the Frensense engine to AI coding agents over the
[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (JSON-RPC on
stdio). Every tool calls the same analysis engine as the CLI: same
lowering, same fact tables, same stable finding IDs.

## Installation

The MCP server is a subcommand of the `frensense` binary. There is no separate
package and no daemon. [Install `frensense`](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/installation), then
check that `frensense mcp` starts (it waits for a client on stdin; press
Ctrl+C to stop). With npm you can also run it without installing:
`npx @friehub/frensense mcp`.

## Registering with your MCP client

MCP clients launch the server themselves as a subprocess over stdio; you
only tell them the command. The binary must be on `PATH`, referenced by
absolute path, or invoked via `npx`.

**Option A: Zero-install via npx (Claude Desktop / Cursor / Cline):**

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "frensense": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@friehub/frensense", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

**Option B: Installed binary (Claude Desktop):**

**Claude Code:**

```bash
claude mcp add frensense -- frensense mcp
```

**Claude Desktop** (`claude_desktop_config.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "frensense": {
      "command": "frensense",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {
        "FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE": "/path/to/frensense-corpus.frc"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Cursor / Zed / any MCP-capable client**: point the command at the
binary; no extra flags needed.

`FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` is optional and session-wide: set it once in the
server env and every tool call merges those learned facts into the
built-in tables automatically. `frensense_scan_file` and
`frensense_diff` also accept a per-call `corpus_bundle` argument that
overrides the environment value for that single call.

## The three tools

### `frensense_audit`: is this tree clean?

Directory-level audit. Best for "scan the whole project before you commit".

```json
{ "name": "frensense_audit",
  "arguments": { "path": "src", "severity_threshold": "warning" } }
```

Arguments:

| argument | type | default | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | **required** | File or directory to audit |
| `severity_threshold` | `critical` | `warning` | `info` | `warning` | Minimum severity to include |
| `language` | string | — | Filter by language (`c`, `go`, `javascript`, `python`, `rust`, `typescript`, `vue`) |
| `corpus_bundle` | string | — | Path to a `.frc` bundle; overrides `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` |
| `stream` | bool | `false` | Emit per-finding `notification` messages as they arrive, then the final result |

Returns `{ "clean": bool, "advisories": [...] }`.

### `frensense_scan_file`: is THIS file clean?

Single-file scan for agent edit loops. Faster and fully scoped; the result
labels every advisory with file/line/column, plus a top-level `stable_ids`
array.

```json
{ "name": "frensense_scan_file",
  "arguments": { "path": "src/pay.py" } }
```

Arguments:

| argument | type | default | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | **required** | Absolute or relative path to one file |
| `severity_threshold` | `critical` | `warning` | `info` | `info` | Minimum severity |
| `min_confidence` | float 0–1 | `0.0` | Minimum engine confidence |
| `corpus_bundle` | string | — | Path to a `.frc` bundle |

Unsupported extensions (`.txt`, `.md`, …) return
`{ "unsupported_file": true, ... }` rather than an error, so the agent can
skip them without exception handling. A nonexistent `path` or
`corpus_bundle` returns an explicit `"error"` field with `clean: false`.

### `frensense_diff`: does MY change introduce findings?

Scans a unified diff and reports **only findings whose line falls inside
the diff's added-line ranges**. Without `diff_text`, it runs
`git diff HEAD` in `repo` and also treats untracked files as all-added
(`git diff` alone never shows untracked files; a brand-new file is exactly
what a gate must not miss).

```json
{ "name": "frensense_diff", "arguments": { "repo": "." } }
```

Or with an explicit patch (works outside any git repository):

```json
{ "name": "frensense_diff",
  "arguments": { "repo": "/work/project", "diff_text": "diff --git a/app.py b/app.py\n--- a/app.py\n+++ b/app.py\n@@ -4,2 +5,3 @@\n def digest(data):\n+    return hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()\n     pass\n" } }
```

Arguments:

| argument | type | default | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `repo` | string | `.` | Repository root; files in the diff are resolved here |
| `diff_text` | string | — | Unified diff text; omit to run `git diff HEAD` in `repo` |
| `severity_threshold` | `critical` | `warning` | `info` | `info` | Minimum severity |
| `min_confidence` | float 0–1 | `0.0` | Minimum engine confidence |
| `corpus_bundle` | string | — | Path to a `.frc` bundle |

The result carries `added_ranges` per file (what the tool considered "the
change"), `files_scanned`, `advisories` filtered to added lines, and their
`stable_ids`.

## End-to-end agent session

A realistic loop: agent edits a file → checks the diff → fixes → verifies
the fix by stable ID. The session below is real output from
v0.7.0-preview.2 against this change to `src/pay.py` in a git repo
(`hash_password` was holding an MD5 password hash and `find_user` built
SQL by concatenation; the agent rewrote both, but also added a new
`hash_token` helper that still uses MD5):

```diff
diff --git a/src/pay.py b/src/pay.py
--- a/src/pay.py
+++ b/src/pay.py
@@ -5,3 +5,3 @@ import sqlite3
 def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
-    return hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest()
+    return hashlib.sha256(password).hexdigest()

@@ -10,3 +10,7 @@ def find_user(conn: sqlite3.Connection, name: str) -> tuple:
     cur = conn.cursor()
-    cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")
+    cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?;", (name,))
     return cur.fetchone()
+
+
+def hash_token(token: str) -> str:
+    return hashlib.md5(token).hexdigest()
```

**1. Gate the change before committing:**

```json
→ {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call",
   "params":{"name":"frensense_diff","arguments":{"repo":"/work/project"}}}
```

```json
← {"clean": false,
   "files_touched": 1, "files_scanned": 1,
   "added_ranges": [{"path": "src/pay.py",
                     "added_ranges": [{"start": 6,  "end": 6},
                                      {"start": 11, "end": 11},
                                      {"start": 13, "end": 16}]}],
   "stable_ids": ["FRN-a441e6e7b795@src/pay.py:16"],
   "advisories": [{ "file_path": "src/pay.py", "line": 16,
                    "title": "Policy violation: weak_hash (hash_token)",
                    "observation": "Weak hash function `md5` ...", ... }]}
```

Note what the gate did: the agent *removed* two findings (the md5 password
hash and the string-concatenated SQL) and *added* one. The diff tool
correctly reports only the added one: pre-existing findings elsewhere in
the file are invisible to this gate, which is exactly what "does my change
introduce findings?" means. `clean: false` with exactly one stable ID is
the signal to iterate.

**2. Fix the flagged function and re-gate:**

```json
→ {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call",
   "params":{"name":"frensense_diff","arguments":{"repo":"/work/project"}}}
```

```json
← {"clean": true, "stable_ids": [],
   "message": "added lines introduce no findings", ...}
```

The change is clean. Compare IDs, not lines: `FRN-a441e6e7b795…` appearing
in step 1 and disappearing in step 2 is proof *that specific finding* was
fixed. The ID is stable across line shifts, so it survives unrelated edits
anywhere above the finding.

**3. Optional: focus on the single file** while iterating (faster than a
diff when the agent is only touching one buffer):

```json
→ {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/call",
   "params":{"name":"frensense_scan_file","arguments":{"path":"src/pay.py"}}}
```

```json
← {"clean": false,
   "file": "/work/project/src/pay.py",
   "stable_ids": ["FRN-a441e6e7b795@/work/project/src/pay.py:16"],
   "advisories": [{ "line": 16,
                    "title": "Policy violation: weak_hash (hash_token)", ... }]}
```

**4. Optional: whole-tree audit** before opening the PR:

```json
→ {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"tools/call",
   "params":{"name":"frensense_audit","arguments":{"path":"src"}}}
```

## Protocol notes

* The server speaks the standard MCP lifecycle: `initialize` →
  `initialized` → tool calls; `shutdown`/`exit` to stop. `tools/list`
  always reflects the current tool set.
* Protocol version: `2024-11-05`.
* Logs go to **stderr**; stdout is protocol-only. Never parse stderr.
* Advisory JSON is the same `Advisory` schema the CLI's `--json` emits
  (fingerprint, taint path steps, tags), so agent-side parsing code works
  for both surfaces.
* A scan failure on one file (syntax errors, unreadable) is reported per
  call as `"error": "..."` with `clean: false`; the agent can retry after
  fixing the file.

* [Editors (LSP)](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/lsp): the same engine inside your editor
* [CI and agent gating](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/github-actions): CI wiring, baseline gating, GitHub annotations
* [CLI reference](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/cli): every flag and exit code

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/lsp.md
description: Run Frensense as a language server so findings appear as editor diagnostics.
---

# Editors (LSP)

`frensense lsp` puts the Frensense engine inside your editor: findings
appear as diagnostics when you open or save a file, with the same severity
mapping, messages, and stable IDs as the CLI and MCP server. It speaks the
standard Language Server Protocol over stdio and ships in the same
`frensense` crate as the CLI and MCP server.

## Installation

`frensense lsp` is a subcommand of the `frensense` binary. There is no editor
extension to install. [Install `frensense`](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/installation) and make
sure it is on the `PATH` your editor sees, then point your editor's generic
LSP client at it (see "Client configuration").

## What it does (and deliberately doesn't)

* Scans on `textDocument/didOpen` and `textDocument/didSave`, publishing
  `textDocument/publishDiagnostics` for that file.
* Scans the **saved file on disk** through the same per-file engine path as
  `frensense watch` and the MCP tools: the engine is the single source of
  truth, so what the editor shows is exactly what CI scans. No in-memory
  AST fork, no incremental-edit replay divergence.
* Diagnostics map advisories 1:1: Critical → Error (1), Warning → Warning
  (2), Info → Information (3); ranges are 0-based; `code` carries the
  stable finding ID (`FRN-…`) and `data` carries the raw fingerprint and
  tags; `source` is `"frensense"`.
* Closing a file clears its diagnostics; unsupported file types clear
  rather than error (closing a deleted file's tab doesn't spam).
* **Diagnostics only.** `initialize` advertises just `textDocumentSync`;
  no hover, completion, or code actions are claimed or supported.

## Client configuration

Any LSP client that launches a stdio server works. Set
`FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` in the server's launch environment if you want
learned `.frc` facts to participate in editor scans — this is read once
when the binary starts, so it must be in the environment the editor passes
to the subprocess, not a shell export after the fact.

### Neovim (built-in LSP, Lua)

```lua
vim.lsp.config('frensense', {
  cmd = { 'frensense', 'lsp' },
  filetypes = { 'python', 'javascript', 'typescript', 'rust', 'go' },
})
vim.lsp.enable('frensense')
```

With a corpus bundle:

```lua
vim.lsp.config('frensense', {
  cmd = { 'frensense', 'lsp' },
  filetypes = { 'python', 'javascript', 'typescript', 'rust', 'go' },
  on_new_config = function(config)
    config.cmd_env = { FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE = '/path/to/frensense-corpus.frc' }
  end,
})
vim.lsp.enable('frensense')
```

### Helix

```toml
# languages.toml
[[language]]
name = "python"
language-servers = ["frensense"]

[language-server.frensense]
command = "frensense"
args = ["lsp"]
environment = { "FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE" = "/path/to/frensense-corpus.frc" }
```

### VS Code (generic LSP client extension)

Point any LSP client extension at the binary:

```json
{
  "frensense.server": {
    "command": "frensense",
    "args": ["lsp"],
    "env": {
      "FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE": "/path/to/frensense-corpus.frc"
    }
  }
}
```

If the binary isn't on `PATH`, use the absolute path (e.g.
`/opt/frensense/frensense`).

## Protocol walkthrough

The transcript below is real v0.7.0-preview.2 output (captured by piping
framed messages into the binary). File on disk:

```python
import hashlib


def digest(data):
    return hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()
```

**1. Client → server: `initialize`** (framed with `Content-Length`):

```
Content-Length: 63

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}
```

**Server → client:** capabilities + server info. Note only
`textDocumentSync` is claimed:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"capabilities":
  {"textDocumentSync":{"openClose":true,"change":1,"save":true},
   "positionEncoding":"utf-16"},
 "serverInfo":{"name":"frensense lsp","version":"0.7.0-preview.2"}}}
```

**2. Client → server:** `initialized`, then open the document:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialized","params":{}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"textDocument/didOpen","params":
  {"textDocument":{"uri":"file:///work/project/app.py",
                   "languageId":"python","version":1,"text":"..."}}}
```

**Server → client:** the diagnostics for the file:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"textDocument/publishDiagnostics","params":
  {"uri":"file:///work/project/app.py",
   "diagnostics":[{
     "range":{"start":{"line":3,"character":11},
              "end":{"line":3,"character":11}},
     "severity":2,
     "code":"FRN-a441e6e7b795@/work/project/app.py:4",
     "source":"frensense",
     "message":"Weak hash function `md5`, not acceptable for passwords or
                security-sensitive digests (use bcrypt/argon2/scrypt or
                SHA-256+)",
     "data":{"fingerprint":"a441e6e7b795f2f2",
             "tags":["checker","weak_hash"]}}]}}
```

Line 3 (0-based) is line 4 (1-based): the editor underline and the CLI's
`app.py:4` are the same position. The `code` is the stable finding ID:
if you insert ten lines above, the underline moves and this string's hash
portion does not change, so issue-tracker references stay valid.

**3. Fix the file and save** (`didSave`): the next publish contains an
**empty** diagnostics array. The finding is gone because the code changed,
not because it was filtered:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"textDocument/publishDiagnostics","params":
  {"uri":"file:///work/project/app.py","diagnostics":[]}}
```

**4. Close the file** (`didClose`): diagnostics are cleared for that URI.
**`shutdown` + `exit`** end the session.

## Combining surfaces

A finding has one identity across every delivery surface:

| surface | where you see it | identity |
|---|---|---|
| editor (LSP) | underline + hover message | `code: "FRN-…"` |
| agent (MCP) | `stable_ids` in tool results | `FRN-…` |
| CI (annotations) | `--github` output on the PR | title + file:line |
| baseline gate | `--compare-baseline` regressions | fingerprint |

An agent can fix a finding the editor flagged and prove it fixed *that*
finding (ID disappears from `frensense_diff` output) without CI ever
seeing a regression.

## Troubleshooting

* **No diagnostics appear**: check the file extension is a supported
  language (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Rust, Go). Unsupported files
  publish empty diagnostics by design.
* **Client logs**: most editors show the server's stderr in an output
  panel (VS Code: *Output → your LSP client*). `frensense lsp` writes scan
  failures there; stdout is protocol-only.
* **Findings differ from the CLI**: make sure both use the same
  `.frc` bundle (`FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` / `--corpus-bundle`); learned
  facts change what the engine can see.
* **`FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` has no effect**: the variable must be set in
  the environment the editor passes when it spawns the `frensense lsp`
  subprocess, not in a shell that is already running.

## Related

* [AI agents (MCP)](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/mcp): the same engine for AI agents
* [CI and agent gating](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/github-actions): CI wiring and baseline gating
* [CLI reference](https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/cli): every flag and exit code

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/bundles.md
description: >-
  What a Frensense bundle is, how to download and use one, and how to judge
  whether it helps on your code.
---

# Bundles (`.frc`)

Frensense ships with a built-in knowledge pack: 1,627 facts about sources,
sinks and sanitizers for the languages it supports. A **bundle** is an extra
pack you load on top, for frameworks and libraries the built-in pack does not
know. If a scan misses a vulnerability because the engine has never heard of
your web framework's request object or database call, a bundle is how you tell
it.

A `.frc` file is a versioned, checksummed archive of two things:

1. **Learned facts**: sources, sinks, sanitizers and policy checks that the
   engine merges into its tables at scan time. A learned sink takes part in the
   same graph analysis as a built-in one, so taint paths and guards apply to it.
2. **Patterns**: vulnerable and fixed examples with their CWE, impact and
   severity, kept so you can see what the bundle was taught from.

A bundle is data, not code. It cannot run anything. It can change what the
engine reports, in both directions (see "Check that a bundle helps").

## Use a bundle

```bash
frensense ./src --bundle my.frc        # -b is the short form
```

Other ways the engine finds one, in the order it looks:

| How | Applies to |
| --- | --- |
| `-b` / `--bundle <file>` on the command line | CLI scans |
| `frensense-corpus.frc` in the scanned folder | CLI scans (found automatically) |
| `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` environment variable | the MCP and LSP servers only |
| `corpus_bundle` argument on an MCP tool call | MCP |

`FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` does not affect a plain `frensense .` scan. Use `-b`
or the auto-discovered file there.

To see what a bundle contains:

```bash
frensense bundle info my.frc          # add --json for machine output
```

## Community bundles

Free starter bundles are published for the main stacks. Each has a datasheet
that lists the classes it covers and the examples it was checked against.

| Bundle | For |
| --- | --- |
| [`frensense-typescript.frc`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/frensense-typescript.frc) | TypeScript and JavaScript (Node.js, Express, Next.js) |
| [`frensense-python.frc`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/frensense-python.frc) | Python (Flask, Django, scripts) |
| [`frensense-go.frc`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/frensense-go.frc) | Go (HTTP handlers, templates, SQL drivers) |
| [`frensense-c.frc`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/frensense-c.frc) | C (memory safety: use after free, leaks, buffer bounds) |
| [`frensense-master.frc`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/frensense-master.frc) | All of the above in one file |

Alongside them:
[`CWE_DATASHEET.md`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/CWE_DATASHEET.md),
[`SHA256SUMS`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/SHA256SUMS) and
its signature
[`SHA256SUMS.sig`](https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/SHA256SUMS.sig).
Check a download before you use it:

```bash
curl -fsSLO https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/frensense-python.frc
curl -fsSLO https://bundles.friehub.cloud/community/latest/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
```

Commercial bundles with broader framework coverage are offered separately.
[Get in touch](https://www.friehub.cloud/contact) for details.

## Check that a bundle helps

More knowledge is not automatically better. A bundle that teaches the engine a
very common function name as a sink can flood a large codebase with false
alarms, and slow the scan down. Before you rely on one in CI, run it against
your own code both ways:

```bash
frensense ./src --json > bare.json
frensense ./src --json -b my.frc > with-bundle.json
```

Compare `advisory_count` in the two files. Then read a sample of the findings
that only the bundle produced and ask whether each one is a real problem. If
most are not, do not use that bundle on this code, and report it so it can be
fixed. A bundle's own datasheet describes the examples it was verified on, not
how it behaves on your project.

## Make your own

You teach the engine with pairs of labelled examples: one vulnerable, one
fixed. The bundler replays each pair through the engine, learns the facts that
separate them, and keeps a fact only if it survives checks against every other
pair. A fact backed by one family is marked `provisional`; two or more make it
`confirmed`.

```bash
frensense lint mycorpus --strict     # check the examples first
frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc     # compile
frensense bundle info my.frc         # read what was actually published
```

Start with [How teaching works](/guide/teachability), then the
[authoring guide](/corpus/authoring).

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/teachability.md
description: >-
  A practical, user-readable guide to understanding and using Frensense's
  teachable static analysis system.
---

# Teachable Static Analysis

Traditional static analysis tools are built like rigid factories: to detect a new vulnerability pattern, someone has to rewrite the machine's internal gears or learn a specialized, obscure query language.

Frensense works differently. It was built with a clear separation between **how code is analyzed** and **what vulnerabilities look like**:

1. **The Engine** (`frensense-engine`): A compiler that parses code into an Intermediate Representation (IR), tracks how values move between variables, inspects branch conditions, and determines data reachability.
2. **The Knowledge Bundles** (`.frc` files): Portable, compiled bundles of security facts that tell the engine which functions are dangerous, which are safe, and what policies must be followed.

Because of this separation, **you do not need to write Rust, understand compiler theory, or recompile the engine** to teach Frensense new vulnerabilities.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Vulnerable Example\n(*_positive)"] --> C["Frensense Bundler\n(Fact Extraction)"]
    B["Remediated Example\n(*_negative)"] --> C
    C --> D["Replay Verification\n(Gate: 0 False Positives)"]
    D --> E["Compiled Knowledge Bundle\n(*.frc)"]
    E --> F["Frensense Scanner\n(--bundle)"]
    G["Target Codebase"] --> F
    F --> H["Accurate Findings\n(Exact Source-to-Sink Path)"]
```

***

## The Twin-Example Method: How Frensense Learns

To teach Frensense, you create a **family** consisting of two files:

* **`[name]_positive.[ext]`**: The vulnerable code containing the dangerous pattern.
* **`[name]_negative.[ext]`**: The safe version showing how the vulnerability was remediated.

### Why Twin Examples Work

When a security vulnerability occurs in production, an engineer writes a pull request to fix it. That pull request contains the exact difference between "dangerous" and "safe":

* Did they add an input validation check?
* Did they switch from raw string concatenation to a parameterized query?
* Did they invoke an authorization check before deleting a record?

The Frensense bundler automatically compares the positive and negative files, identifies what made the difference, and distills it into a **Learned Fact**.

***

## The 13 Teachable Subsystems

Under the hood, Frensense's knowledge system is categorized into 13 distinct security dimensions. Every dimension corresponds to an entry in the engine's `LearnedFactEntry` table:

### 1. Dangerous Sinks (`LearnedFactEntry::Sink`)

A "sink" is a function where untrusted data causes harm (such as executing a system command or running a database query).

* **What is taught**: Which argument slot is dangerous.
* **Real-world benefit**: In `cursor.execute(sql, params)`, slot 0 (`sql`) is dangerous, but slot 1 (`params`) is a safe parameterized binding channel. The engine learns not to flag parameterized queries.

### 2. Untrusted Sources (`LearnedFactEntry::Source`)

A "source" is any place where untrusted user data enters your application.

* **What is taught**: Function calls or object properties that deliver user data (e.g., `request.cookies.get`, `request.body.json`, or custom RPC gateways).

### 3. Sanitizers (`LearnedFactEntry::Sanitizer`)

A "sanitizer" is a function that cleanses data or renders it harmless.

* **What is taught**: Escaping helpers (e.g. `html.escape()`, `quote_plus()`) or type coercions (`int()`, `float()`) that remove risk.

### 4. Data Propagators (`LearnedFactEntry::Propagator`)

A "propagator" transforms data while preserving its untrusted nature.

* **What is taught**: Encoding/decoding helpers like `base64.b64decode`, string formatters, or array manipulation functions.

### 5. Security Policies (`LearnedFactEntry::Policy`)

Policies enforce that certain security checks must happen in the same function or module as a sensitive operation.

* **What is taught**: "Whenever function `delete_user()` is called, function `verify_admin_role()` must precede it."

### 6. Non-Dataflow Checks (`LearnedFactEntry::Check`)

Direct code structure inspection that does not require tracking variable flows.

* **What is taught**: Detecting calls to deprecated APIs or configuration functions missing mandatory flags.

### 7. Memory Contracts (`LearnedFactEntry::MemoryContract`)

Tracks heap allocation and deallocation across boundaries in systems languages (C, C++, Rust).

* **What is taught**: Which functions allocate new memory and which functions consume/free pointers, preventing use-after-free bugs.

### 8. Cryptographic Standards (`LearnedFactEntry::WeakCrypto`)

Enforces corporate cryptography standards.

* **What is taught**: Flagging weak hash algorithms (`md5`, `sha1`, `des`) while allowing secure algorithms (`sha256`, `argon2id`).

### 9. Authorization Guards (`LearnedFactEntry::GuardBypass`)

Recognizes authorization and containment checks.

* **What is taught**: Helper functions that validate whether a requested resource belongs to the current user or tenant.

### 10. Schema Validation (`LearnedFactEntry::SchemaPolicy`)

Recognizes input validation frameworks (such as Zod, Yup, or Pydantic).

* **What is taught**: Acknowledging that data passing through schema validator methods is validated.

### 11. Syntax Roles (`LearnedFactEntry::GrammarRole`)

Teaches the parser how new or unusual language syntax functions without modifying the engine.

* **What is taught**: Mapping language AST nodes to functions, variables, or call expressions dynamically.

### 12. Syntax Features (`LearnedFactEntry::GrammarFeature`)

Teaches language idioms like object destructuring, template literals, and ternary operators.

* **What is taught**: Enabling accurate variable tracking through modern JavaScript or Python language features.

### 13. Access Control & Multi-Tenancy (`LearnedFactEntry::IdorFinderSink`)

Detects Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR).

* **What is taught**: Database query methods and required multi-tenant ownership keys (e.g., `account_id`, `tenant_id`).

***

## Step-by-Step: How to Teach Frensense in Practice

### Step 1: Create a Corpus Folder

Create a directory with positive and negative code snippets:

```bash
mkdir -p my_corpus/py/authz.missing/py_custom_auth
```

Create `py_custom_auth_positive.py` (the bug). The `[frensense]` block carries
what every report shows and what the lint checks:

```python
# [frensense]
# observation: An invoice is fetched by id with no check that it belongs to the caller's organization.
# impact: Any authenticated user can read another organization's invoices by guessing ids.
# improvement: Scope the lookup to the caller's organization id.
# cwe: CWE-639
# severity: high
# class: authz.missing
# purpose: knowledge
# shape: unscoped-idor-lookup
# source: synthetic: minimal reproduction of the unscoped lookup
# VULNERABLE: Direct lookup without tenant scoping
def get_invoice(req):
    invoice_id = req.args.get("id")
    return db.query_invoice(invoice_id)
```

Create `py_custom_auth_negative.py` (the fix):

```python
# SAFE: Scoped lookup requiring active organization ID
def get_invoice(req):
    invoice_id = req.args.get("id")
    org_id = req.session.get("org_id")
    return db.query_invoice(invoice_id, org_id=org_id)
```

A `bug_classes.json` at the corpus root declares `authz.missing` (CWE-639 plus
its parent CWE-862 as `related_cwe`).

### Step 2: Lint and Build the Bundle

```bash
frensense lint my_corpus --strict     # metadata, layout, diversity, teachability
frensense bundle my_corpus my_company.frc
frensense bundle info my_company.frc  # what the bundle actually carries
```

The lint refuses the pair before a bundle exists if the metadata is incomplete
or the family would teach nothing (`PU004`). The bundler then extracts the fact,
runs the **replay verification gate** across both files, and writes the binary
`my_company.frc` bundle. The full contract - required keys, the fact shapes a
family can teach, held-out pairs and every lint code - is the
[corpus authoring guide](/corpus/authoring).

### Step 3: Scan with Your Knowledge Bundle

Provide the bundle to the scanner:

```bash
frensense src/ --bundle my_company.frc
```

Or drop `frensense-corpus.frc` directly into the root directory of your project; Frensense will discover and load it automatically.

***

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need to know Rust to teach Frensense?

**No.** All training examples are written in the target language of your application (Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, C, Rust). The bundler handles all analysis and translation into binary knowledge bundles.

### What happens if a learned rule conflicts with built-in rules?

Knowledge bundles are designed with safe precedence:

* **Learned facts win on specific knowledge**: If a bundle teaches that a specific parameter is safe, that precision overrides generic defaults.
* **Narrow facts cannot be widened**: A generic rule cannot overwrite a precise, slot-restricted signature.

### How does Frensense prevent false alarms from learned rules?

Before any rule is written into an `.frc` bundle, it must pass the **Replay Gate**. The candidate rule is tested against all negative examples in the corpus. If it causes even a single false positive on safe code, the bundler rejects it.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/corpus.md
---
# Corpus & .frc bundles

The corpus is a set of **labelled example families**. Each family contains at
least one *positive* (vulnerable) example and one *negative* (fixed) example.
The bundler replays each family through the engine, diffs the two variants,
learns facts that distinguish them, then verifies those facts against every
other family before publishing them into a `.frc` bundle.

```
mycorpus/
├── bug_classes.json                  # class registry the lint checks against
└── ts/inj.sql/ts_sqli/
    ├── ts_sqli_positive.ts           # [frensense] metadata block at the top
    ├── ts_sqli_negative.ts           # fixed version, starts with "SAFE:"
    ├── ts_sqli_heldout_positive.ts   # blind pair: never read by the bundler
    └── ts_sqli_heldout_negative.ts
```

The `<family>_positive.<ext>` / `<family>_negative.<ext>` infix is what makes a
family; a directory with `positive.ts` and `negative.ts` groups **zero**
families. Supported extensions: `ts`, `tsx`, `js`, `jsx`, `py`, `go`, `rs`,
`c`, `h`. (C++ files are not analysed by the engine, so C++ examples teach it nothing.)

## Lint, build, inspect

```bash
# 1. Pre-flight: metadata, layout, provenance, diversity, teachability.
frensense lint mycorpus --strict

# 2. Compile the families into a bundle.
frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc

# 3. Read what was actually published.
frensense bundle info my.frc
```

`frensense lint` never scans target code unless you ask it to, and it refuses
the mistakes the replay gate cannot see: a mislabelled class, copied families,
placeholder advisory prose, and a pair that would teach nothing (`PU004`).
`frensense bundle` is the current spelling of the old `frensense-bundler`
invocation that took a corpus and an output path.

## Use the bundle

See [Bundles](/bundles#use-a-bundle) for the ways to load one and how to check it helps.

  the nine fact shapes a family can teach, held-out pairs, the lint codes,
  verified command output, and a migration checklist for families written
  against the old guide.
